claim: Did you know… a Martian meteorite appeared to contain fossilized bacteria?

studies.finding: Carbonate globules, magnetite grains, organic molecules and tiny rod shapes in meteorite ALH84001 were presented as possible traces of ancient Martian life.
studies.verdict: Each feature has since been explained without biology; no convincing evidence of life.

claim: Did you know… the clouds of Venus may contain a gas made by life?

studies.finding: Radio telescopes detected an absorption line attributed to phosphine in the Venusian clouds, a gas with no known non-biological source there.
studies.verdict: Original calibration questioned; later telescopes and reanalyses disagree about whether any signal exists.

studies.finding: A reanalysis of the same observations found no phosphine, and noted a nearby sulfur dioxide line could mimic the feature.
studies.verdict: Greaves et al. replied that a signal remains; the dispute is unresolved.

claim: Did you know… the first interstellar visitor could be an alien light sail?

studies.cite: Bialy & Loeb (2018), The Astrophysical Journal Letters
studies.finding: A thin sheet pushed by sunlight could explain why 'Oumuamua sped up slightly as it left the Sun's vicinity.
studies.verdict: Most astronomers favor a natural origin; hydrogen outgassing offers one such explanation.

studies.finding: Hydrogen trapped in water ice by radiation, then released on heating, could supply the observed push.
studies.verdict: Plausible natural account; other natural explanations still compete.

claim: Did you know… a star dimmed so oddly that astronomers raised alien megastructures?

studies.cite: Boyajian et al. (2016), Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
studies.finding: Citizen scientists spotted a star whose brightness dipped deeply and irregularly, unlike typical stellar behavior.
studies.verdict: The megastructure idea circulated widely; it is disfavored but no explanation covers everything.

studies.cite: Boyajian et al. (2018), The Astrophysical Journal Letters
studies.finding: New dips dimmed blue light more than red, which an opaque object cannot do.
studies.verdict: Points to dust, though the dust's origin remains open.

claim: Did you know… the Large Hadron Collider glimpsed a particle nobody ordered?

studies.finding: A search of 8 and 13 TeV collisions found a modest excess of photon pairs near 750 GeV.
studies.verdict: Not a particle; chance fluctuation.

studies.finding: With more 13 TeV data, a search for high-mass photon pairs saw no significant excess.
studies.verdict: The bump vanished with more data, after many theory papers.

claim: Did you know… a lead compound was announced as a room-temperature superconductor?

studies.finding: A copper-doped lead apatite was reported as a superconductor at room temperature and ambient pressure, with partial levitation as evidence.
studies.verdict: Not superconducting; purer samples are insulators.

studies.finding: A copper sulfide impurity undergoes a transition near 104 C that mimics the resistance drop and heat-capacity anomaly.
studies.verdict: Explained the apparent signal; no zero resistance was ever shown.

claim: Did you know… dark matter may rise and fall with the seasons?

studies.cite: Bernabei et al. (2013), European Physical Journal C
studies.finding: A sodium iodide detector in Italy recorded a yearly modulation in low-energy events over seven cycles, matching the pattern expected from dark matter.
studies.verdict: Not reproduced by other sodium iodide experiments; origin unexplained.

studies.finding: Six years of data from a similar detector showed no annual modulation of the kind DAMA/LIBRA reported.
studies.verdict: Challenges the DAMA/LIBRA claim at over 3 sigma.

claim: Did you know… distant icy bodies point to an unseen ninth planet?

studies.finding: Six distant Kuiper belt objects share clustered orbits, which a planet roughly ten Earth masses far beyond Neptune could explain.
studies.verdict: No planet has been seen; clustering may be an observing artifact.

studies.cite: Shankman et al. (2017), The Astronomical Journal
studies.finding: After accounting for survey biases, a dedicated survey found the distant objects' orbits consistent with random orientation.
studies.verdict: Challenges the clustering; the authors of the claim dispute this.

claim: Did you know… a tiny island human species lived until 50,000 years ago?

studies.finding: Skeletal remains from Liang Bua cave on Flores were assigned to a new, small-bodied, small-brained hominin species.
studies.verdict: Disease explanations such as Down syndrome were rejected; species status stands.

studies.finding: Revised stratigraphy dated the youngest bones to about 60,000 years ago, much earlier than first reported.
studies.verdict: Revised the date, not the species.

claim: Did you know… a new human lineage was identified from one finger bone?

studies.finding: Mitochondrial DNA from a juvenile's finger bone in a Siberian cave belonged to a hominin lineage distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans.
studies.verdict: Confirmed by nuclear genomes and later fossils; Denisovans are established.

studies.finding: Nuclear DNA showed the Denisovans were related to Neanderthals and contributed genes to present-day Melanesians.
studies.verdict: Replicated; Denisovan ancestry is found in many living populations.

claim: Did you know… the Moon is wreckage from a planet that hit Earth?

studies.finding: Simulations showed that a Mars-sized body striking the early Earth could eject enough material to form the Moon.
studies.verdict: Leading explanation; the Moon's Earth-like isotopes remain a puzzle.
